analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers a rising fee for carbon pollution and sends the money to every taxpayer as a monthly dividend.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require coal producers, oil refiners, and natural gas sellers to buy federal permits for the carbon their products would emit, starting at $12.50 per ton in 2016 and rising on a published schedule toward a national target of cutting emissions to 20% of 2005 levels by 2060 [S2, S3]. All permit revenue would go into a new trust fund that pays an equal monthly dividend to every lawful U.S. resident taxpayer, with half-shares for up to two dependents [S2, S3]. The bill also places an equivalent fee on imports of carbon-intensive goods like steel, cement, and aluminum so foreign producers don't gain an edge, and refunds fees to exporters [S2, S3]. It was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees in February 2015, sent to an Energy and Power subcommittee, and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Most American households come out ahead on paper: because the dividend is paid per person rather than per dollar of energy use, lower-income families, who use less energy than the wealthy, would generally receive more in dividends than they pay in higher fuel and electricity prices [S3]. Taxpayers collectively receive the entire permit revenue stream as monthly checks [S2, S3]. Renewable energy, efficiency, and low-carbon industries gain because their products carry no permit fee, making them cheaper relative to fossil fuels [S3]. Future generations gain from a legislated path cutting U.S. emissions roughly 80% below 2005 levels by the 2056-2060 period [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: Every lawful resident taxpayer would receive an equal monthly dividend from the permit revenue, so the money collected from carbon-intensive fuels is returned to the public rather than kept by the Treasury [S3].

The permit price starts at $12.50 per ton of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2016 and follows a published five-year schedule with a floor and ceiling, giving energy producers and consumers a predictable, escalating price signal to shift away from coal, oil, and gas [S3].

The bill sets hard emission targets: national emissions averaging no more than 90% of 2005 levels in 2016-2020, stepping down to 20% of 2005 levels in 2056-2060, and the Treasury must raise or lower permit prices to hit those targets [S2, S3].

An equivalency fee on imported carbon-intensive goods — steel, aluminum, cement, glass, paper, chemicals, and similar products — mirrors the cost domestic producers pay, protecting U.S. factories from plants in countries with no carbon price, and exporters receive equivalent refunds [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal producers, oil refinery operators, and first sellers of natural gas pay the permit fees on every ton their products would emit, and they pass much of that cost to consumers through higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity [S2, S3]. Anyone who fails to buy a required permit owes a penalty tax of 100% of the unpaid permit amount [S3]. Households that use large amounts of energy — drivers of long commutes, homes heated with fuel oil, energy-intensive manufacturers — pay more in higher prices than they receive back in dividends [S3]. Coal-mining regions would face the steepest pressure as the price schedule makes coal progressively more expensive relative to other fuels.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy energy users

drawbacks.text: Energy prices would rise immediately when the fee takes effect, while dividends arrive monthly; households and businesses would face higher gasoline, heating, and electricity costs from day one, and anyone whose energy use is far above average receives less in dividends than they pay in higher prices [S3].

Coal communities and fossil-fuel-dependent regional economies would absorb concentrated harm: the escalating minimum and maximum permit prices — reaching a minimum of $118.75 and a maximum of $131.25 by 2025, adjusted for inflation — are designed to make coal progressively uneconomic, with no dedicated transition assistance for miners or coal towns in the bill [S3].

The bill concentrates enormous price-setting power in the Treasury Department, which sets the permit price each year with only a floor-and-ceiling band, an approach opponents of carbon pricing criticize for giving an executive agency control over energy costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design addresses the main fairness objection to a carbon price by rebating 100% of revenue as equal per-person dividends, which leaves most lower- and middle-income households net winners while charging heavy energy users. The trade-off is real: energy costs rise for everyone before any dividend arrives, the transition squeezes coal regions with no transition aid in the bill, and the target schedule is aggressive enough that the required permit prices climb steeply within a decade. A good-faith supporter can call the dividend mechanism the fairest way to price carbon; a good-faith opponent can object that it still raises living costs for rural and driving-heavy households and hands price control to Treasury.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees in February 2015 and to an Energy and Power subcommittee a week later, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2017 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott (D-WA) introduced the Managed Carbon Price Act on February 13, 2015 [S1, S5].
The bill was referred to two committees — Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce — on the day of introduction, splitting jurisdiction between the tax-writing panel and the energy panel [S5].
On February 20, 2015, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy and Power [S5].
Three Democratic House members cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor signed on [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the 114th Congress, which ended January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and electric utilities never faced the carbon fee, and energy prices stayed on their pre-existing path. The status quo — no federal carbon price at all — continued through 2017, so the industries the bill would have charged are better off, and no household ever received the dividend.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers avoided the carbon fee

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all recorded support — the sponsor and three cosponsors — was Democratic, and the Republican-controlled committees took no action [S4, S5].

industries.note: Coal mined in the United States, including lignite and peat, would carry a permit fee on every ton of carbon it would emit when burned, with prices escalating to a minimum of $118.75 per ton by 2025 [S3]. The industry avoided this only because the bill never advanced; had it passed, coal would have been the first fuel priced out under the targets [S3].

industries.industry: Oil refiners and petroleum product makers
industries.note: Refinery operators would buy permits for the carbon in every barrel and product received, costs passed to consumers at the pump [S2, S3]. The industry's interest was in the bill never moving, which is what happened [S5].

industries.industry: Natural gas producers and first sellers
industries.note: First sellers of natural gas would pay the same permit fees, though gas emits less carbon per unit of energy than coal, so the bill shifts relative economics in gas's favor even as it raises gas costs [S3].

industries.industry: Import-sensitive manufacturers (steel, aluminum, cement, glass, paper, chemicals)
industries.note: The bill taxes their energy inputs but pays exporters a refund and charges an equivalency fee on competing imports, insulating U.S. producers from countries without a carbon price [S2, S3].
Wind, solar, and efficiency carry no permit fee, so a rising fossil-fuel price makes them progressively more competitive [S3].
